corrected_value.title: Thar She Bursts: Reducing Confusion Reduces Bubbles
corrected_value.title_o: Thar She Bursts: Reducing Confusion Reduces Bubbles

decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of Thar She Bursts: Reducing Confusion Reduces Bubbles by Kirchler, M./Huber, J./Stöckl, T. (2012) in: The American Economic Review, 102(2), pp. 865–883. Replication Authors: Anna Dreber, Siri Isaksson and Magnus Johannesson Kirchler et al. compare mispricing in experimental asset markets under constant fundamental value with declining fundamental value. Mispricing is higher under a declining fundamental value. Hypothesis to bet on: A declining fundamental value (FV) increases mispricing in experimental asset markets (a comparison of the mean relative absolute deviation (RAD) between treatment 1 (t1) and treatment 2 (t2)).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (Kirchler et al., 2012), line 1337 (see also Reference 48, lines 316-317, and Table S2, lines 1200-1202)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record (row 2103) and blind coding (target 15) correctly identify Kirchler, Huber, and Stöckl (2012), 'Thar She Bursts: Reducing Confusion Reduces Bubbles', American Economic Review 102(2), 865-883 (Ref. 48) as the replicated original study.

decisions.quote: As planned 220 observations were collected in the replication. The purpose of the replication is to replicate the difference in the relative absolute deviation (RAD) between treatment t1 (a declining fundamental value (F V ) and increasing cash to asset value ratio (C/A)) and treatment t2 (a constant F V and an increasing C/A). In the original study RAD is 0.414 in treatment t1 and 0.079 in treatment t2 and this difference (the effect size) of 0.355 is significant (p = 0.016 with a Mann-Whitney test). These results are shown in Table 1 below (which is a reproduction of the second row in Table 6 on page 875 in the original paper for the replication data). In the replication RAD is 0.157 in treatment t1 and 0.049 in treatment t2. This difference (the effect size) of 0.108 is significant using the same test as in the original study (p = 0.010). The original result is thus replicated, consistent with that a declining fundamental value increases mispricing (i.e prices different than the F V ). The relative effect size of the replication is 30.42% (0.108/0.355).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (Kirchler et al., 2012), Replication Results, line 1337 (and Table S1, line 1270)
decisions.reason: The individual primary project replication report for Kirchler, Huber, and Stöckl (2012) and Table S1 (line 1270, 'Replicated: Yes') state an explicit overall verdict that the focal RAD hypothesis was replicated at p = 0.010 ('The original result is thus replicated' and in Discussion: 'Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%'). Although the report also notes 'For completeness' that relative deviation (RD) was not significant, under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1 and the Coding Rules the explicit overall verdict on the pre-specified central hypothesis governs, confirming 'successful'.

decisions.quote: This replication will be performed at the Goethe University Frankfurt, in 2015, on students at the University of Frankfurt, while the original data was gathered at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, in 2009–2010. As in the original study we will include Bachelor and Master students in business administration and/or economics, but if needed the recruitment will be extended to bachelor and masters students in other fields. Individuals that have participated in other asset market experiments will be excluded. The experiment will be in German as in the original study. The original study also looks at variation in the cash-to asset value (constant or increasing) and a different context, but the focus of the replication is on the difference between constant and declining fundamental value. Replication Results As planned 220 observations were collected in the replication.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (Kirchler et al., 2012), Differences from Original Study and Replication Results, line 1337
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from 220 students at Goethe University Frankfurt to re-test the published finding of Kirchler, Huber, and Stöckl (2012), making it a replication.

decisions.reason: Both the shipped record (row 2104) and blind coding (target 14) correctly identify J. B. Kessler and A. E. Roth (2012), 'Organ allocation policy and the decision to donate', American Economic Review 102(5), 2018 (Ref. 47) as the replicated original study.

Although the standalone individual report for Kessler and Roth (2012) is not among the 14 appended project reports, the main study's Supplementary Table S1 explicitly attributes an author replication verdict to Kessler and Roth (AER 2012, Ref. 47): Replication P-value = 0.016, Replication Effect Size (r) = 0.34 (vs. Original P-value < 0.001, Original Effect Size r = 0.49), and 'Replicated: Yes' (relative effect size 0.71). Both shipped and blind coding rightly record the outcome as 'successful'.

decisions.quote:
1. Replications
We replicate 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2014 in the high-
impact general interest journals the American Economic Review (AER) and the Quarterly
Journal of Economics (QJE). (33–50) The deadline for inclusion in the study was that the
paper should be published or posted as accepted/in press at the website of the journal at
August 1, 2014.
decisions.reason: The study conducts a new-sample laboratory experiment (N = 48 in the replication vs. N = 288 in the original, Table S1 line 1269) re-testing the between-subjects organ donation priority treatment effect of Kessler and Roth (2012) (Ref. 47, within Refs. 33-50), which is a replication.
